title: Home Workouts vs. the Gym: Which One You'll Actually Stick To
description: Dumbbells at home or a gym membership? We compare real costs, results, and the thing that decides it: where you'll still be training in four months.
excerpt: At home you get zero commute. At the gym you get real weight and a head that's switched on. The difference isn't price — it's where you actually show up.
content:
Nearly everyone hits the same fork: buy some dumbbells for the flat, or pay for a gym? The answer isn't about money. It's about where you'll realistically train three times a week four months from now, once the January energy has worn off.

## What it actually costs

A decent home setup — adjustable dumbbells, a bench, a mat — runs roughly $400 to $900. A gym is $30–60 a month, so the home kit pays for itself in about a year and a half. That math only works if you use it. An unused bench under the bed is the most expensive fitness equipment ever made.

## Where the real difference is

Home wins on time: no commute, and you can train at 6am in whatever you slept in. It loses on load. The moment you want to squat 200lb, you need a rack, a bar and plates — different money, different amount of floor space.

The gym has a second advantage people rarely mention: the mental switch. Walk through the door and you're there for one reason. At home the laundry, the kid, or a notification will always find you.

## The mix that works

For most people the answer is both: short bodyweight and band sessions at home on tight days, plus two proper barbell sessions a week. That only works if you can get into a gym whenever your day allows — not just in the 6-to-8pm queue.

That's what [GymHome](https://gymhome.cz) is built for: book a slot online, a code opens the door, and the space is yours. Run the mix for two weeks and you'll know which half you need more of.
